record.tranche_reason: The study measures and illustrates polysemantic behaviour in GPT2-small using neuron embeddings and clustering, a different method from the original neuron visualisation work. It also tests a neuron-embedding loss on a toy MLP SAE.
record.gate_note: The paper reports examples of GPT2-small neurons with multiple semantic clusters, aggregate embedding-distance comparisons, and toy SAE results. The explanation of superposition in Related Work is background, not a tested result. The study does not report a systematic count of polysemantic neurons or layer-by-layer prevalence. Results cited from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper. It takes polysemanticity as given and reports how well its neuron-embedding clustering and neuron-embedding (NE) SAE loss perform. The GPT2-small neurons (R1, R2) are hand-picked illustrations. The paper counts no share of polysemantic neurons, compares no layers, and does not show whether the mixed behaviours are unrelated. It describes the common case as 'related but distinct' behaviours. R3/R4 compare its own representation against pre-MLP embeddings. R5–R10 measure SAE neurons, not the model's own neurons, under a loss built to reduce the study's own proxy. So none of the results bear on any version as stated.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that neuron embeddings separate a neuron's dataset examples into distinct behaviours and give proxy measures of polysemanticity useful for evaluating SAEs. On a toy MNIST MLP, the NE loss appears to trade reconstruction accuracy and activation sparsity for higher monosemanticity (by their proxy) and far fewer dead neurons. They stress this is early-stage work on a toy model and that transfer to larger models is unclear.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses element-wise products of pre-MLP embeddings and neuron input weights, followed by clustering and geometric metrics, rather than the original neuron-visualisation approach. It also introduces a neuron-embedding loss for SAE training.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper states that examining examples further down the activation spectrum can reveal more behaviours, including rare secondary behaviours. Aggregate cluster distances also differ between pre-MLP and neuron embeddings.

fits_no_version.finding: A GPT2-small layer-7 neuron splits into six behaviour clusters, some semantically related. The authors say related-but-distinct behaviours are quite common in GPT2-small, but give no count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Many GPT2-small MLP neurons show several related but distinct behaviours (offshoots of one job) rather than unrelated ones (anecdotal; would bear on V6 if quantified).

fits_no_version.finding: In one neuron, the primary behaviour outnumbers a rare secondary behaviour almost 50:1 among examples above 75% of maximum activation. The authors say reviewing few examples would make it look monosemantic.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Judging a neuron monosemantic depends on how many activating examples are reviewed (illustrative; near V7 but not tested).

fits_no_version.finding: Adding a neuron-embedding loss to an SAE on a toy MNIST MLP lowers the study's embedding-distance proxy. It also raises reconstruction MSE, accuracy loss and L0, and sharply reduces dead neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A monosemanticity-targeting SAE loss trades reconstruction and sparsity for lower embedding-distance polysemanticity proxies.

record.peer_reviewed: PMLR 235, 2024 (printed in the paper); venue supplied as arXiv.org
record.problems: The GPT2-small analysis uses 10,000 OpenWebText inputs, selects examples at a 75% maximum-activation threshold, and caps examples at 100 per neuron; it does not quantify polysemantic-neuron prevalence or report layer-by-layer results. The SAE training experiment is a proof of concept on a toy MNIST MLP, and the authors say transfer to larger models is unclear. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3's size (7 to 32) and dead-neuron percentage (23.8% to 3.7%) are reported training outcomes but do not directly measure the claim versions' polysemantic behaviour or its prevalence. Other qualitative neuron visualisations are not separate measured outcomes for the versions recorded.

untested.parts: No share of GPT2-small MLP neurons that are polysemantic, no layer comparison, and no test of whether the behaviours are unrelated. Only selected example neurons are shown.
Superposition is mentioned only as background in Related Work.
Initialization, regularization and training noise are not tested as causes.
No comparison of activation functions or architectures in the base model. The only intervention is an SAE loss on a toy MNIST MLP, evaluated by the study's own proxy.
No systematic test of whether mixed neurons share one feature. The 'related but distinct' remark is anecdotal.
Activation thresholds and explanation-scoring methods are not varied. The paper only argues that reviewing few top examples can miss rarer behaviours.

record.verdict_notes: The reader labelled this paper tests/T2 with supports verdicts on V2, V5 and V7. I downgraded it to T4: the GPT2 examples are method demonstrations with no prevalence, the V7-like point is an argument from a single neuron, and the SAE results measure the study's own loss on its own proxy, on SAE neurons. If the panel prefers counting R1 for V2, it is at most cannot_determine for a 'large share' and gives no information on unrelatedness.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not quantify the share of all MLP neurons that are polysemantic, compare layers, or report a systematic distribution over unrelated tokens or contexts.
Superposition is discussed as a proposed explanation, but the study does not test whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity.
The paper does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemanticity when capacity is sufficient.
The study tests a neuron-embedding loss on a toy MNIST MLP SAE only; it does not compare activation functions, modern convnets, or large language models.
The examples are not a systematic test of whether canonical mixed-response neurons detect one shared feature or whether truly unrelated mixtures are rare.

The study does not compare multiple explanation-scoring systems or systematically vary activation thresholds; it does discuss how examples lower in the activation spectrum can reveal additional behaviours.
